comparator.name: Law in Society
comparator.sourceNotes: The English-taught full-time programme has ten compulsory 6 EC units in each of years one and two. Year three has 30 EC of open study, three 6 EC Recap courses and a 12 EC thesis. The Recap courses require 36 EC from eight specified legal and thematic units. Thesis entry requires Evaluation Research and 30 EC from specified legal, thematic and Recap units. The current thesis course lists Public Law and Terrorism separately where the regulations combine them typographically. Thesis assessment combines an individual legal and empirical study with a group empirical component and poster. English diagnostic completion or the refresher gates the Diversity grade. Professional and Personal Identity coaching carries no credits. Approved alternative elective or exchange packages are subject to course level and approval rules. Civiel Effect requires a separate Dutch preparatory pathway and a qualifying law master.

core: Law used as an instrument to analyse and address social challenges, integrating public, private and criminal law around societal problems
Human rights, justice and the philosophical/ethical foundations of law
Combining legal analysis with sociological and psychological perspectives on institutions and behaviour
Empirical legal-social research: quantitative statistics and qualitative methods used to evaluate law and design policy
International law, EU law and global governance, including migration governance
Security, terrorism and criminal justice examined through law, philosophy and psychology
Negotiation, mediation and dispute resolution applied to legal-social problems
adjacent: Sustainability, climate and corporate responsibility, including environmental governance and the ethics of AI/technology
Globalisation of markets, the platform economy and worker/consumer protection
questions: How can law and policy evaluation improve responses to global challenges such as migration, security, sustainability and market globalisation?
How should companies and digital platforms be held accountable for environmental harm and for the treatment of workers and consumers?

trace: Case law, trial simulations and legal/social/normative perspectives establish the integrated law-and-society foundation.
Human-rights treaties, monitoring/case law and natural-law philosophy connect legal protection to justice and ethical argument.
Sociological theories and institutions, race/gender and colonial contexts provide a social explanation of the settings in which law operates.
Research design, sampling, operationalisation, inference/ANOVA and a group project supply empirical methods for investigating law-related social questions.
Social influences on judgments, attitudes and behaviour supply the psychological perspective needed to interpret legal actors and public responses.
Compares international relations theories and applies them to global political and institutional cases.
Studies AI ethics and human interaction, including fairness, privacy and responsibility.
Venture ideation, market validation and business planning explain how firms formulate transactions and commercial models later examined in transnational/platform-business law; not legal doctrine.
Criminal accountability, guilt, legality, punishment and simulated legal advice implement substantive criminal-law reasoning; criminological causation remains limited.
Comparative property, tort and contract principles and their social pressures supply the private-law strand of the legal response.
Climate mechanisms, social effects, justice and mitigation establish the factual background for evaluating legal/governance climate responses; not treaty or corporate climate law.
Cross-border contracts, trade, intellectual property, foreign investment and digital commerce provide substantive transnational business-law analysis.
BATNA/ZOPA, bargaining structures, trade-offs and negotiation simulations provide dispute-negotiation skills; mediation procedure is not assumed.
Examines sources and institutions of public international law, including human rights, responsibility, force and environmental protection.
Comparative constitutional/administrative principles, state power and rights supply public-law reasoning across legal systems.
EU institutions, legislative dossiers and organised-interest research explain the political process through which legal rules and economic policies are formed.
Consumer/firm incentives, market structure and aggregate economic effects explain behaviour of actors regulated in platform/transnational-business settings; not legal protection itself.
Theoretical tools, knowledge, responsibility and rigorous argumentation support reflective legal/normative reasoning; not a dedicated philosophy-of-law course.
Uses research on youth radicalisation, risk and protective factors to inform educational prevention.
Research design, interviews/meaning, data interpretation and reflexivity supply qualitative methods before later applied empirical work.
EU legal institutions, rights, citizenship and free movement analysed through cases/PBL supply the multilevel European-law strand.
Conflict causes, violence, structural inequality and peacebuilding/reconciliation explain social problems addressed by security and justice institutions; not criminal doctrine.
Rule-making, governmental/nonstate actors, interests and sustainability policy/enforcement supply governance analysis complementary to environmental law; not professional legal ethics.

alternatives.label: Law, justice and global governance
alternatives.concept: Study public, private, criminal, international and human-rights law alongside social research and political science. Use negotiation, comparative legal reasoning and empirical methods to examine how legal institutions respond to questions about security, markets and global governance. Climate science and sustainability governance help explain the problems that legal responses address.
alternatives.labelReason: The courses combine substantive legal reasoning across fields with social and empirical inquiry into institutions, rights and conflict.
progression: Law, Society & Justice precedes the advanced law courses. The business and statistics gateways precede Transnational Business Law and Negotiation & Strategic Thinking. Each term has four offered courses.

selection.assessment: The legal and social research option combines eight legal courses with quantitative and qualitative research, sociology, psychology, negotiation and international governance. Environmental science and business courses give the legal questions context. A separate sustainability and markets option can study policy, firms and environmental impacts, but lacks a distinct sequence in platform regulation, climate law or evaluation of legal interventions. Adding the same legal core would repeat the primary option without establishing a separate legal focus.

blocks: Security, criminal justice and legal philosophy
VU requires a dedicated criminology course on explaining, measuring and responding to crime.
VU studies defamation and assault as specific legal problems.
VU examines diversity within the programme’s legal and social context.
Both develop empirical research design and statistical reasoning. UCR applies these skills in a group research project.
Both connect law to philosophical questions about rights and justice. UCR concentrates on human-rights law and its foundations.
Both use psychology to explain behaviour. UCR focuses on social influence, attitudes and group processes.
VU teaches dedicated legal and security perspectives on terrorism. UCR studies youth resilience and educational prevention.
Globalisation of markets and business law
Both examine law and cross-border markets. UCR focuses on transactions, contracts and digital commerce, while VU also studies public and private actors in the platform economy.
Migration, qualitative methods and dispute resolution
Both study international rules and institutions. UCR covers a range of fields in public international law, with migration as one context.
VU studies migration law and the nation state in a dedicated course.
Both teach qualitative research design, data collection and interpretation. UCR applies these methods in social research.
Both introduce sociological theory and institutions. UCR provides tools for examining identity, inequality and social change.
Both teach negotiation through practice. UCR develops bargaining and strategic analysis, while VU also addresses mediation and dispute resolution.
Sustainability, technology ethics and applied evaluation research
Both examine ethical and social questions about AI. UCR focuses on fairness, privacy and responsibility, while VU also examines technical approaches and legal uses.
VU applies legal frameworks to climate change. UCR provides climate science and policy context.
VU examines ethical questions that legal professionals face in sustainability work.
VU studies multinationals and legal issues in the platform economy.
VU requires a separate statistics course using SPSS.
VU requires a dedicated course on evaluating interventions.
VU uses Amsterdam as a setting for applied sociolegal sustainability research.
Personal development, private/public-law recap, thesis and elective space
Both develop private-law reasoning through comparative study of property, obligations and liability.
Both examine public law and constitutional institutions. UCR compares legal systems, state power, judicial review and rights.
Both study substantive criminal law and legal reasoning. UCR introduces criminal liability and punishment, while VU integrates prior study in a Recap course.
VU requires a 12 EC thesis that combines legal and empirical research. UCR’s optional independent research is outside the schedule.
VU reserves 30 EC for approved open study.

notes.text: UCR brings together law, social research and governance. VU provides more specialist work in migration, terrorism, platform markets and climate law, and requires a legal and empirical thesis. Dutch professional qualification through Civiel Effect has separate requirements.

audience.programmeDescription: VU Law in Society integrates public, private and criminal law with social sciences and empirical inquiry. Security, migration, sustainability and global markets organise study of how legal approaches address societal problems.
audience.comparisonExplanation: The UCR option combines substantive law courses with sociology, psychology, research methods and negotiation. VU provides dedicated legal study of migration, terrorism, platform markets and climate change, alongside evaluation research and a compulsory thesis.

curriculum.limitation: The 180 EC curriculum includes 30 EC of open study and a 12 EC thesis. The Recap courses and thesis have separate entry requirements. Professional and Personal Identity coaching carries no credits.
